units.title: Challenges
units.intro: Grammar: finite and non-finite clauses, and understanding complex sentences.

cards.title: Finite and non-finite clauses
rule: A **finite clause** has a verb that shows tense and agrees with a subject: *She **faces** many challenges.* *Because he **was** ill, ...*

A **non-finite clause** has no tense; its verb is a **to-infinitive**, an **-ing participle** or a **past participle**: ***To succeed**, you must work hard.* ***Facing** many problems, she never gave up.* ***Given** enough time, we can solve it.*
The subject of a participle clause must be the same as the main clause subject: *Walking home, **I** saw an accident* (I was walking).

examples.text: Having finished the exam, she went home.
Walking to school, the rain started.
examples.fix: Walking to school, I was caught in the rain.

examples.text: To pass the exam, you need to revise.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following sentences exhibits the correct English word order ($$\text{S-V-O}$$)?

steps.text: English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object ($$\text{S-V-O}$$) pattern.
The subject is 'The security guard', the verb is 'locked', and the direct object is 'the main gate'.
Option A and Option C place the verb ('locked') at the end of the clause, which is an $$\text{S-O-V}$$ pattern typical of Tigrinya grammar (ሓላው ሰላም ማዕጾ ዓጸዎ) and represents a common L1 transfer error.

cards.answer: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb error caused by L1 interference.

steps.text: Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires an explicit copula verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the predicate nominative.
In Option C, the copula verb 'is' is completely missing.

In Tigrinya, the copula can sometimes be omitted or structurally merged, leading students to translate "ሓወይ ኣብቲ ዓዲ ትጉህ ሓረስታይ [እዩ]" directly as "My brother a hardworking farmer..." without including the essential English copula 'is'.

cards.answer: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence that correctly manages sentence boundaries without creating a comma splice.

options.A: The rain was heavy, we decided to stay indoors.
options.B: The rain was heavy we decided to stay indoors.
options.C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.
options.D: Because the rain was heavy, so we decided to stay indoors.

cards.why:

A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined with only a comma. Option A is a comma splice. Option B is a run-on sentence. Option C uses a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb ('therefore'), which is structurally perfect.

cards.q: Complete the sentence with the correct word order: 'The school principal ________.'

options.A: yesterday welcomed the new students warmly
options.B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday
options.C: welcomed yesterday warmly the new students
options.D: the new students welcomed warmly yesterday

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
English adverbs of manner ('warmly') usually precede the main verb or follow the object. Adverbs of time ('yesterday') belong at the end of the sentence. The correct structure is: Subject ('The school principal') + Adverb of Manner ('warmly') + Verb ('welcomed') + Object ('the new students') + Adverb of Time ('yesterday').

cards.title: Understanding long sentences
rule: To understand a long sentence: (1) find the **main clause** (subject + finite verb); (2) put brackets around subordinate and non-finite clauses; (3) ask what each bracket adds (time, reason, condition, purpose).

examples.text: [Although tired,] the farmers [working in the fields] continued.
Main clause here: the farmers continued.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Finite clauses have a tensed verb and a subject; non-finite clauses use to-infinitives, -ing or past participles and borrow their subject from the main clause. To read complex sentences, find the main clause first.
